chunks.section: A Margin Perspective on LoRA: Robustness to Catastrophic Forgetting and Adapter Merging (MaLoRA)
chunks.text: Ziqing Xu 1,4 Hancheng Min 7 Lachlan Ewen MacDonald 3,4 Salma Tarmoun 2,4 Enrique Mallada 8 Weijie Su 1 René Vidal 2,3,4,5,6 1 Statistics and Data Science 2 AMCS 3 ESE 4 IDEAS 5 Radiology 6 CIS University of Pennsylvania 7 INS & SMS, Shanghai Jiao Tong University 8 ECE, Johns Hopkins University † † thanks: Correspondence: ziqingxu@wharton.upenn.edu

Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is the de facto method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large neural networks, achieving strong task adaptation with minimal trainable parameters and low optimization cost. Beyond this efficiency, practitioners have observed two striking properties: robustness to catastrophic forgetting and the ability to merge independently trained adapters into a single model that performs competitively across multiple tasks. These properties are central to continual and multi-task learning, yet remain poorly understood. In this work, we provide a theoretical explanation through a unified margin-based perspective . We analyze LoRA in multiclass linear classification under a near-orthogonal task regime with ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -regularization, and characterize the optimal LoRA adapter across regularization regimes. Our analysis shows that, in an intermediate regime of regularization parameters, the optimal adapter aligns with the max-margin solution on the fine-tuning data. Building on this characterization, we derive two key consequences. First, we obtain closed-form expressions for the margins on pre-training and fine-tuning data, revealing a precise margin trade-off: the regularization parameter controls the balance between retention and adaptation. Second, we analyze adapter merging, proving that merged models achieve positive margin on each task and deriving optimal mixing coefficients that balance margins across tasks and maximize the margin over their union. These results lead to a simple, training-free merging rule, which we term margin-based LoRA merging (MaLoRA). Experiments on modern architectures and real datasets validate our theoretical predictions, showing that MaLoRA matches or outperforms several adapter-merging baselines across a range of

ing (MaLoRA). Experiments on modern architectures and real datasets validate our theoretical predictions, showing that MaLoRA matches or outperforms several adapter-merging baselines across a range of vision and language classification tasks.

Foundation models have transformed artificial intelligence across numerous domains. However, deploying these models in real-world applications typically requires fine-tuning on specialized datasets to meet accuracy, safety, and alignment requirements. Traditional full fine-tuning, which updates all parameters of a pre-trained model, incurs substantial computational cost, including large memory footprints, long training times, and significant storage demands. Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) addresses this challenge by augmenting pre-trained weight matrices W W with low-rank adapters B , A B,A while keeping W W frozen. Empirically, LoRA matches the performance of full fine-tuning while training only a small fraction of the parameters. While LoRA was originally introduced for its computational efficiency, practitioners have since identified two striking empirical properties. 1. Robustness to catastrophic forgetting. In fine-tuning and continual learning, the degradation of performance on previously learned tasks after adapting to new ones (a.k.a. catastrophic forgetting) is a fundamental challenge ( McCloskey and Cohen, 1989 ; Kirkpatrick et al., 2017 ; Ramasesh et al., 2021 ) . Surprisingly, recent studies show that LoRA exhibits strong robustness to catastrophic forgetting, even after substantial adaptation ( Wistuba et al., 2023 ; Biderman et al., 2024 ; Qiao and Mahdavi, 2024 ) . This robustness makes LoRA particularly appealing for continual learning.

2. Effective adapter merging. In multi-task settings, maintaining separate fine-tuned models for each task is storage-intensive. Remarkably, LoRA adapters trained independently on different tasks can be merged (e.g., via simple weighted averaging) into a single adapter that performs well across all tasks ( Huang et al., 2023 ; Yadav et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Yu et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2024 ) . This property enables flexible and efficient deployment. Despite these empirical benefits, the theoretical mechanisms underlying LoRA’s robustness to catastrophic forgetting and its adapter merging capabilities remain poorly understood. In this work, we provide a unified theoretical explanation for both phenomena through a margin-based perspective. Paper contributions. We study LoRA in multiclass linear classification under a near-orthogonal-task regime, in which fine-tuning samples are nearly orthogonal to one another and to the pre-training samples. In this setting, we characterize the global minimizer of the LoRA objective and use this characterization to analyze forgetting and adapter merging. Compared with prior theoretical work on LoRA (see Appendix B ), our work makes the following contributions: • Characterization of the optimal solution. We characterize the global minimizer of LoRA across different regularization regimes (Theorem 3.1 ). In the high-penalty regime, the optimal adapter is zero. In the intermediate regime, the adapter aligns with the max-margin direction on the fine-tuning data. In the low-penalty regime, the adapter aligns with a non-max-margin classifier whose direction generally does not admit a simple closed form. Nevertheless, we show that this direction converges to an interpretable limit as the regularization parameter tends to zero.

• Theory for reduced forgetting. We define forgetting as the reduction in margin on the pre-training data after fine-tuning, and derive closed-form expressions for the normalized margins on the pre-training data, the fine-tuning data, and their union (Theorem 3.2 ). Our analysis shows that these margins are governed by the regularization parameter and satisfy a precise trade-off: decreasing the regularization parameter increases the fine-tuning margin but also increases the Frobenius-norm ratio of the adapter to the pre-trained weights, leading to greater forgetting. We further identify the regularization parameter that maximizes the margin on the union of pre-training and fine-tuning tasks, thereby optimally balancing retention and adaptation. • Theory for adapter merging. Under the intermediate-regime assumption for each task, we derive closed-form expressions for the margin of the merged model on every task (Theorem 3.3 ). We show that the merged model attains strictly positive margin on each task, providing a theoretical explanation for the effectiveness of adapter merging. We also characterize, in closed form, the mixing coefficients that maximize the margin of the merged model on the union of all tasks, which naturally leads to margin-based LoRA merging (MaLoRA), a theoretically motivated adapter-merging method. This contrasts with many existing model-merging approaches, which rely primarily on heuristic prescriptions for choosing how to combine task-specific models.

• Numerical validation. Experiments on real datasets and modern architectures support the theory in three ways: (i) in the linear probing setting, the empirically optimal regularization parameter agrees with the value predicted by our analysis; (ii) in the same setting, the empirically optimal adapter mixing weights agree with our closed-form coefficients; and (iii) in LoRA adapter merging, MaLoRA achieves performance comparable to, and in several cases better than, strong heuristic adapter-merging baselines across vision and language classification tasks.

In this section, we first introduce the multiclass linear classification problem and its corresponding hard-margin SVM formulation. We then describe the specific learning problem considered in this work, which consists of a pre-training and fine-tuning phase. Finally, we state the key assumptions that underpin our analysis, and discuss their motivation and implications.

We first review the standard K K -class linear classification problem. Given a dataset 𝒟 \mathcal{D} , the goal is to learn a weight matrix W ∈ ℝ K × d W\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times d} that minimizes the mean empirical cross-entropy loss: min W ∈ ℝ K × d ⁡ L ⁡ ( W , 𝒟 ) := 1 | 𝒟 | ​ ∑ ( 𝒙 , 𝒚 ) ∈ 𝒟 ℒ CE ​ ( 𝒚 , W ​ 𝒙 ) , \displaystyle\textstyle\min_{W\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times d}}L(W;\mathcal{D}):=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{(\bm{x},\bm{y})\in\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}(\bm{y},W\bm{x}), (1) where 𝒙 ∈ ℝ d \bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is the input and 𝒚 ∈ ℝ K \bm{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{K} is a one-hot label vector. The cross-entropy loss is given by: ℒ CE ( 𝒚 , 𝒚 ^ ) := − ∑ c = 1 K y c log ( exp ⁡ ( y ^ c ) ∑ i = 1 K exp ⁡ ( y ^ i ) ) , 𝒚 ^ = W 𝒙 . \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}(\bm{y},\hat{\bm{y}}):=-\sum_{c=1}^{K}y_{c}\log\!\left(\frac{\exp(\hat{y}_{c})}{\sum_{i=1}^{K}\exp(\hat{y}_{i})}\right),\qquad\hat{\bm{y}}=W\bm{x}\,. (2) Recent studies have shown that when the data are linearly separable, gradient descent (GD) implicitly biases the solution of ( 1 ) toward the max-margin classifier ( Soudry et al., 2018 ; Lyu and Li, 2019 ; Ravi et al., 2024 ) . Specifically, the iterates of GD converge in direction to the max-margin solution of the following hard-margin SVM problem 1 1 1 Whenever ( 3 ) is feasible, its solution is unique since the objective ‖ W ‖ F 2 \|W\|_{F}^{2} is strongly convex and the feasible set is convex. : W SVM ​ ( 𝒟 ) := arg ​ min W ∈ ℝ K × d ⁡ ‖ W ‖ F 2 subject to C ⁡ ( W , 𝒟 ) ≥ 1 , \displaystyle W^{\mathrm{SVM}}(\mathcal{D}):=\argmin_{W\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times d}}\|W\|_{F}^{2}\quad\text{subject to}\quad C(W;\mathcal{D})\geq 1, (3) where C ⁡ ( W , 𝒟 ) C(W;\mathcal{D}) is the minimum margin over the dataset:

C ⁡ ( W , 𝒟 ) := min ( 𝒙 , 𝒚 ) ∈ 𝒟 ⁡ min k ≠ c , y c = 1 ⁡ ( 𝒘 c ⊤ ​ 𝒙 − 𝒘 k ⊤ ​ 𝒙 ) , with W = [ 𝒘 1 ; … ; 𝒘 K ] ⊤ . \displaystyle\textstyle C(W;\mathcal{D}):=\min_{(\bm{x},\bm{y})\in\mathcal{D}}\;\min\limits_{k\neq c,y_{c}=1}\left(\bm{w}_{c}^{\top}\bm{x}-\bm{w}_{k}^{\top}\bm{x}\right),\quad\text{with}\quad W=[\bm{w}_{1};\dots;\bm{w}_{K}]^{\top}. (4) The hard-margin SVM problem in ( 3 ) seeks a weight matrix of minimum norm that separates all examples with at least unit margin between the correct class and the nearest competing class. Intuitively, classification decisions depend primarily on the direction of the weight matrix rather than its scale. To enable comparisons across different scales of W W , we adopt the normalized margin used in ( Crammer and Singer, 2001 ) , i.e., γ ⁡ ( W , 𝒟 ) := C ⁡ ( W , 𝒟 ) ‖ W ‖ F \textstyle\gamma(W;\mathcal{D})\!:=\!\frac{C(W;\mathcal{D})}{\|W\|_{F}} for W ≠ 0 W\neq 0 . This definition has been used in recent theoretical studies ( Lyu and Li, 2019 ; Ravi et al., 2024 ) . We additionally set γ ⁡ ( 0 , 𝒟 ) := 0 \gamma(0;\mathcal{D})\!:=\!0 by convention.

We now describe the specific pre-training and fine-tuning framework used in our theoretical analysis. Pre-training stage. Let 𝒟 pre \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pre}} be a labeled dataset with K K classes, and let W pre ∈ ℝ K × d W_{\mathrm{pre}}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{K\times d} denote a pre-trained linear classifier obtained by GD minimizing the cross-entropy loss L ⁡ ( W , 𝒟 pre ) L(W;\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pre}}) . When 𝒟 pre \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pre}} is linearly separable, this objective admits no finite minimizer. The GD iterates instead diverge in norm while converging in direction to the max-margin solution ( Lyu and Li, 2019 ; Soudry et al., 2018 ) . We formalize this directional structure in Assumption 2.4 . Fine-tuning stage. We adapt the pre-trained model to a downstream dataset 𝒟 ft \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{ft}} consisting of n n additional samples from each of 2 ≤ K ¯ ≤ K 2\leq\bar{K}\leq K classes selected from the original K K pre-training classes. This restriction applies throughout the paper and appendix, including to every task in adapter merging. This setup captures practical scenarios such as domain-incremental learning ( Esaki et al., 2024 ) , domain adaptation ( Zohrizadeh et al., 2019 ; Zhang et al., 2022 ) , and bias-rebalancing fine-tuning ( Li and Xu, 2021 ; ValizadehAslani et al., 2024 ) . When LoRA is applied to adapt the pre-trained model to the fine-tuning task, we introduce a low-rank update to the weights, parameterized by matrices B ∈ ℝ K × r B\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times r} and A ∈ ℝ r × d A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d} : min B , A ⁡ L ⁡ ( W pre + B ​ A , 𝒟 ft ) + λ 2 ​ ( ‖ B ‖ F 2 + ‖ A ‖ F 2 ) . \displaystyle\textstyle\min_{B,A}\;L(W_{\mathrm{pre}}+BA;\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{ft}})+\frac{\lambda}{2}(\|B\|_{F}^{2}+\|A\|_{F}^{2}). (5)

Here, the Frobenius-norm penalties explicitly constrain the adapters in weight space, limiting the deviation of the fine-tuned model from the pretrained initialization. Although some empirical studies of LoRA do not include this penalty explicitly in the loss, they train the adapters using the AdamW optimizer ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017 ) , whose decoupled weight decay induces an effect analogous to L 2 L_{2} regularization on B B and A A . Thus, the objective in ( 5 ) captures the regularization that is, explicitly or implicitly, used in standard LoRA fine-tuning practice ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Wistuba et al., 2023 ; Biderman et al., 2024 ) . Our goal is to understand the structure of the optimal solution to ( 5 ), and how it explains both LoRA’s robustness to catastrophic forgetting and its effectiveness in enabling adapter merging.

Our theoretical analysis uses the following assumptions. Let N ft = K ¯ ​ n N_{\mathrm{ft}}\!=\!\bar{K}n be the number of fine-tuning samples, write X ft = [ 𝒙 ¯ 1 , … , 𝒙 ¯ N ft ] X_{\mathrm{ft}}\!=\![\bm{\bar{x}}_{1},\ldots,\bm{\bar{x}}_{N_{\mathrm{ft}}}] , and let X pre X_{\mathrm{pre}} collect the pre-training feature vectors as columns.

The combined pre-training and fine-tuning datasets are linearly separable. (6)

In the strict-orthogonal case ϵ 1 = ϵ 2 = 0 \epsilon_{1}\!=\!\epsilon_{2}\!=\!0 , the input dimension satisfies d ≥ N ft + rank ⁡ ( X pre ) d\!\geq\!N_{\mathrm{ft}}\!+\!\operatorname{rank}(X_{\mathrm{pre}}) . For near-orthogonal data, we assume ( N ft − 1 ) ​ ϵ 1 < 1 (N_{\mathrm{ft}}\!-\!1)\epsilon_{1}\!<\!1 .
The LoRA rank parameter satisfies r ≥ K ¯ r\!\geq\!\bar{K} , where K ¯ \bar{K} is the number of fine-tuning classes.

The pre-trained classifier W pre W_{\mathrm{pre}} is a scaled version of the hard-margin SVM solution on 𝒟 pre \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pre}} : W pre = ρ pre ⋅ W pre SVM / ‖ W pre SVM ‖ F W_{\mathrm{pre}}\!=\!\rho_{\mathrm{pre}}\!\cdot\!W_{\mathrm{pre}}^{\mathrm{SVM}}/\|W_{\mathrm{pre}}^{\mathrm{SVM}}\|_{F} , for some scalar ρ pre > 0 \rho_{\mathrm{pre}}\!>\!0 , where W pre SVM = W SVM ​ ( 𝒟 pre ) W_{\mathrm{pre}}^{\mathrm{SVM}}\!=\!W^{\mathrm{SVM}}(\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pre}}) .

Assumption justification. The near-orthogonal task Assumption 2.1 is arguably a strong assumption in practice, but reflects the realistic geometric structure of fine-tuning data, and similar orthogonality-type assumptions are commonly used in theoretical analyses to enable closed-form characterizations ( Bui Thi Mai and Lampert, 2021 ; Boursier et al., 2022 ; Frei et al., 2022 ; Kou et al., 2023 ) . The feature-correlation analyses on CIFAR-100 and six multi-domain benchmarks in Appendices H.1.1 and H.2.1 provide empirical motivation for studying this reference geometry. Assumption 2.2 makes the geometric feasibility and conditioning requirements explicit. The strict-case bound accounts for both the fine-tuning sample count and the pre-training feature span, specifying a high-dimensional, sample-limited setting. Assumption 2.3 requires only r ≥ K ¯ r\!\geq\!\bar{K} , meaning the LoRA rank needs only to be at least the number of fine-tuning classes. Finally, Assumption 2.4 is motivated by recent theoretical results on the implicit bias of GD in multiclass classification ( Lyu et al., 2021 ; Ravi et al., 2024 ) , as discussed in § 2.1 . ρ pre \rho_{\mathrm{pre}} captures the (unspecified) scale at which pre-training was stopped, which arises naturally in implicit-bias analyses where the GD iterate diverges along the SVM direction. For clarity of exposition, all theorems in the main paper are stated under the strict-orthogonal special case ( ϵ 1 = ϵ 2 = 0 \epsilon_{1}\!=\!\epsilon_{2}\!=\!0 ) of Assumption 2.1 . The general versions of these results for ϵ 1 , ϵ 2 > 0 \epsilon_{1},\epsilon_{2}\!>\!0 , together with their proofs, are deferred to the Appendix D – F .

Implications. The assumptions introduced above lead to a clean closed-form expression for the K ¯ \bar{K} -class hard-margin SVM solution for the fine-tuning task, and also imply near-orthogonality between the pre-trained weights W pre W_{\mathrm{pre}} and the fine-tuning dataset 𝒟 ft \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{ft}} , which underpins our subsequent theoretical analysis in § 3 . To formalize these implications, we begin by introducing the concept of a simplex equiangular tight frame (simplex ETF), which characterizes the geometry of the hard-margin SVM solution in our setting

For m ≥ 2 m\!\geq\!2 , an m m -simplex ETF is a collection of m m vectors in ℝ p \mathbb{R}^{p} for some p ≥ m p\!\geq\!m , given by the columns of M m := m m − 1 ​ P ​ ( 𝐈 m − 1 m ​ 𝟏 m ​ 𝟏 m ⊤ ) M_{m}\!:=\!\sqrt{\frac{m}{m-1}}\,P\left(\bm{I}_{m}\!-\!\frac{1}{m}\bm{1}_{m}\bm{1}_{m}^{\top}\right) , where P ∈ ℝ p × m P\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times m} satisfies P ⊤ ​ P = 𝐈 m P^{\top}P\!=\!\bm{I}_{m} . Throughout, we use the canonical choice p = m p\!=\!m and P = 𝑰 m P\!=\!\bm{I}_{m} , so M m ∈ ℝ m × m M_{m}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{m\times m} . Using this definition, we now present a proposition that, under the strict-orthogonal specialization, characterizes the structure of the hard-margin SVM solution for the fine-tuning data ( 𝒟 ft \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{ft}} ) and the orthogonality between the pre-trained weights ( W pre W_{\mathrm{pre}} ) and the fine-tuning data.

Let K ¯ ≥ 2 \bar{K}\!\geq\!2 . Under Assumption 2.1 with ϵ 1 = ϵ 2 = 0 \epsilon_{1}\!=\!\epsilon_{2}\!=\!0 and Assumption 2.4 , the following hold: (i) The minimum-norm SVM solution W ft SVM ∈ ℝ K ¯ × d W_{\mathrm{ft}}^{\mathrm{SVM}}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{\bar{K}\times d} for 𝒟 ft \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{ft}} , defined by ( 3 ) with K ¯ \bar{K} output classes, admits the closed-form solution W ft SVM = K ¯ − 1 K ¯ ​ ( M K ¯ ⊗ 𝟏 n ⊤ ) ​ X ft ⊤ W_{\mathrm{ft}}^{\mathrm{SVM}}\!=\!\sqrt{\frac{\bar{K}\!-\!1}{\bar{K}}}\left(M_{\bar{K}}\!\otimes\!\bm{1}_{n}^{\top}\right)X_{\mathrm{ft}}^{\top} , where 𝒙 i , j \bm{x}_{i,j} is the j j -th sample from class i i , and X ft = [ 𝒙 1 , 1 , … , 𝒙 1 , n , … , 𝒙 K ¯ , n ] X_{\mathrm{ft}}\!=\![\bm{x}_{1,1},\dots,\bm{x}_{1,n},\dots,\bm{x}_{\bar{K},n}] is the fine-tuning data matrix. (ii) The pre-trained weights are orthogonal to the fine-tuning data: W pre ​ 𝒙 ¯ = 0 W_{\mathrm{pre}}\bm{\bar{x}}=0 for all 𝒙 ¯ ∈ 𝒟 ft \bm{\bar{x}}\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{ft}} .

Remark on Proposition 2.1 . Proposition 2.1 reveals that the hard-margin SVM solution for the fine-tuning task admits a compact closed-form expression: W ft SVM = K ¯ − 1 K ¯ ​ ( M K ¯ ⊗ 𝟏 n ⊤ ) ​ X ft ⊤ W_{\mathrm{ft}}^{\mathrm{SVM}}\!=\!\sqrt{\frac{\bar{K}-1}{\bar{K}}}\left(M_{\bar{K}}\otimes\bm{1}_{n}^{\top}\right)X_{\mathrm{ft}}^{\top} . However, this form does not immediately reveal how the classifier aggregates information from the fine-tuning data. To provide insight, we explicitly derive the expression for the first row of W ft SVM W_{\mathrm{ft}}^{\mathrm{SVM}} (the remaining rows follow symmetrically), yielding ( K ¯ − 1 K ¯ ​ ∑ i = 1 n 𝒙 ¯ 1 , i − 1 K ¯ ​ ∑ k = 2 K ¯ ∑ j = 1 n 𝒙 ¯ k , j ) ⊤ . \textstyle\left(\frac{\bar{K}-1}{\bar{K}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bm{\bar{x}}_{1,i}-\frac{1}{\bar{K}}\sum_{k=2}^{\bar{K}}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bm{\bar{x}}_{k,j}\right)^{\top}. Intuitively, each row of W ft SVM W_{\mathrm{ft}}^{\mathrm{SVM}} encodes a direction that emphasizes its corresponding class mean while uniformly suppressing the influence of all other classes, leading to class separation in max-margin classification. The second result in Proposition 2.1 follows from the representer theorem for SVMs, which implies that the hard-margin SVM solution on pre-training data lies in the span of 𝒟 pre \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pre}} . By Assumption 2.4 , W pre W_{\mathrm{pre}} inherits this property; combined with condition (c) of Assumption 2.1 at ϵ 2 = 0 \epsilon_{2}\!=\!0 , each row of W pre W_{\mathrm{pre}} is therefore orthogonal to the fine-tuning data.

Building upon these assumptions and propositions, we develop a rigorous theoretical framework that provides a principled explanation for LoRA’s empirical advantages in the subsequent section. Our analysis reveals properties that enable precise quantification of LoRA’s benefits in terms of robustness to catastrophic forgetting and adapter merging performance.

In this section, we first analyze the optimization landscape of the LoRA objective and characterize its global minimum in § 3.1 . We then derive closed-form expressions for the margins on the union of pre-training and fine-tuning datasets, explaining why LoRA mitigates catastrophic forgetting in § 3.2 . Finally, in § 3.3 , we extend our margin-based analysis to the multi-task setting, explaining the effectiveness of adapter merging and deriving optimal mixing coefficients that maximize the margin on the union of all tasks. Moreover, building on these closed-form coefficients, we translate them into a simple training-free merging rule, margin-based LoRA merging (MaLoRA, Algorithm 1 ).

Effect of regularization and connection with max-margin classifier. The theorem shows that the regularization parameter governs the structure of the optimal LoRA adapters. In the high-penalty regime , the regularization term dominates and drives the optimal adapters to zero. In the intermediate regime , the adapters balance cross-entropy and regularization, yielding the explicit form in ( 8 ). In particular, the first K ¯ \bar{K} rows of B λ ∗ ​ A λ ∗ B_{\lambda}^{\ast}A_{\lambda}^{\ast} align with the K ¯ \bar{K} -class hard-margin SVM solution on the fine-tuning data (Proposition 2.1 ), which gives a clear max-margin interpretation of the learned solution. In the low-penalty regime , explicit formulas for a λ a_{\lambda} and b λ b_{\lambda} are no longer available. Nevertheless, as λ → 0 + \lambda\to 0^{+} , the cross-entropy term dominates and Θ λ → ∞ \Theta_{\lambda}\to\infty , while our asymptotic analysis still characterizes the limiting direction of B λ ∗ ​ A λ ∗ B_{\lambda}^{\ast}A_{\lambda}^{\ast} in ( 9 ). This direction coincides with the hard-margin SVM solution only when K ¯ = K \bar{K}=K .

chunks.section: 3.2 Margin trade-off between forgetting and fine-tuning under LoRA adaptation
chunks.text: We now analyze catastrophic forgetting through the normalized margin. Our goal is to characterize how the LoRA fine-tuned model trades off performance on the pre-training data and the fine-tuning data as the regularization parameter varies, and to identify the regularization level that maximizes the margin on their union. For convenience, define γ pre := γ ⁡ ( W pre , 𝒟 pre ) , γ ft , λ := γ ⁡ ( B λ ∗ ​ A λ ∗ , 𝒟 ft ) \gamma_{\mathrm{pre}}\!:=\!\gamma(W_{\mathrm{pre}};\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pre}}),\gamma_{\mathrm{ft},\lambda}\!:=\!\gamma(B_{\lambda}^{\ast}A_{\lambda}^{\ast};\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{ft}}) . Moreover, we define the adaptation to the fine-tuning data and forgetting on the pre-training data by Adapt ⁡ ( λ ) = γ ⁡ ( W LoRA λ , 𝒟 ft ) − γ ⁡ ( W pre , 𝒟 ft ) , Forget ⁡ ( λ ) := γ pre − γ ⁡ ( W LoRA λ , 𝒟 pre ) . \displaystyle\mathrm{Adapt}(\lambda)\!=\!\gamma\bigl(W_{\mathrm{LoRA}}^{\lambda};\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{ft}}\bigr)\!-\!\gamma(W_{\mathrm{pre}},\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{ft}}),\quad\mathrm{Forget}(\lambda)\!:=\!\gamma_{\mathrm{pre}}\!-\!\gamma\bigl(W_{\mathrm{LoRA}}^{\lambda};\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pre}}\bigr)\,. (12) Based on these definitions, we now present the theorem.

Adopt the setup of Theorem 3.1 under strict orthogonality, and assume K ¯ = K ≥ 2 \bar{K}=K\!\geq\!2 . Let γ ft ∗ \gamma_{\mathrm{ft}}^{\ast} be the max normalized margin any linear classifier can obtain on the fine-tuning data 𝒟 ft \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{ft}} , and recall the scalar ρ pre \rho_{\mathrm{pre}} from Assumption 2.4 . Then, Adapt ⁡ ( λ ) \mathrm{Adapt}(\lambda) and Forget ⁡ ( λ ) \mathrm{Forget}(\lambda) can be characterized uniformly over all λ \lambda as follows: Adapt ⁡ ( λ ) = γ ft , λ ​ Θ λ Θ λ 2 + ρ pre 2 , Forget ⁡ ( λ ) = γ pre ​ ( 1 − ρ pre Θ λ 2 + ρ pre 2 ) . \displaystyle\mathrm{Adapt}(\lambda)\!=\!\gamma_{\mathrm{ft,\lambda}}\,\frac{\Theta_{\lambda}}{\sqrt{\Theta_{\lambda}^{2}+\rho_{\mathrm{pre}}^{2}}}\,,\quad\mathrm{Forget}(\lambda)=\gamma_{\mathrm{pre}}\biggl(1-\frac{\rho_{\mathrm{pre}}}{\sqrt{\Theta_{\lambda}^{2}+\rho_{\mathrm{pre}}^{2}}}\biggr)\,. (13) Moreover, the effect of the regularization parameter λ \lambda is characterized by two regimes: (i) High-penalty regime: if λ ≥ 1 K ¯ ​ n \lambda\!\geq\!\frac{1}{\bar{K}\sqrt{n}} , then Θ λ = 0 \Theta_{\lambda}\!=\!0 , and hence Forget ⁡ ( λ ) = Adapt ⁡ ( λ ) = 0 \mathrm{Forget}(\lambda)\!=\!\mathrm{Adapt}(\lambda)\!=\!0 . (ii) Intermediate and low-penalty regimes: if λ < 1 K ¯ ​ n \lambda\!<\!\frac{1}{\bar{K}\sqrt{n}} , then γ ft , λ = γ ft ∗ \gamma_{\mathrm{ft},\lambda}\!=\!\gamma_{\mathrm{ft}}^{\ast} , and Θ λ \Theta_{\lambda} is decreasing in λ \lambda . Therefore, Adapt ⁡ ( λ ) \mathrm{Adapt}(\lambda) and Forget ⁡ ( λ ) \mathrm{Forget}(\lambda) are both decreasing in λ \lambda . In particular,

lim λ → 0 + ( Adapt ⁡ ( λ ) , Forget ⁡ ( λ ) ) = ( γ ft ∗ , γ pre ) , lim λ → 1 K ¯ ​ n ( Adapt ⁡ ( λ ) , Forget ⁡ ( λ ) ) = ( 0 , 0 ) . \displaystyle\lim_{\lambda\to 0^{+}}\bigl(\mathrm{Adapt}(\lambda),\mathrm{Forget}(\lambda)\bigr)\!=\!\bigl(\gamma_{\mathrm{ft}}^{\ast},\gamma_{\mathrm{pre}}\bigr),\quad\lim_{\lambda\to\frac{1}{\bar{K}\sqrt{n}}}\bigl(\mathrm{Adapt}(\lambda),\mathrm{Forget}(\lambda)\bigr)\!=\!(0,0). (14)

Notably, the intermediate and low-penalty regimes coincide when K ¯ = K \bar{K}=K . This merging is specific to the case K ¯ = K \bar{K}\!=\!K ; when K ¯ < K \bar{K}\!<\!K , the two regimes remain distinct. Balancing adaptation and forgetting. Theorem 3.2 shows that the same quantity Θ λ \Theta_{\lambda} controls both adaptation and forgetting. As λ \lambda decreases, the adapter scale Θ λ \Theta_{\lambda} increases, improving Adapt ⁡ ( λ ) \mathrm{Adapt}(\lambda) on the fine-tuning data while also increasing Forget ⁡ ( λ ) \mathrm{Forget}(\lambda) on the pre-training data. Thus, LoRA fine-tuning induces a direct margin trade-off: stronger adaptation comes at the cost of larger pre-training margin degradation. The natural question is how to choose λ \lambda to balance these effects. In the following Corollary 3.1 , we quantify this trade-off by studying the normalized margin on the union of the pre-training and fine-tuning datasets, which leads to an explicit optimal regularization level.

In particular, it shows that the optimal mixing coefficients are given by the ratio between the unnormalized margin of the pre-trained model on 𝒟 pre \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pre}} and that of each fine-tuned adapter on its own task. The unnormalized margin measures how confidently a classifier separates classes on its dataset, with smaller values indicating more challenging classification problems. This formula admits a direct interpretation: an adapter that achieves a smaller margin on its task is assigned a larger mixing weight, increasing its contribution so as to

ing classification problems. This formula admits a direct interpretation: an adapter that achieves a smaller margin on its task is assigned a larger mixing weight, increasing its contribution so as to preserve a positive margin for that task in the merged model.

The preceding analysis suggests choosing adapter mixing coefficients according to how confidently each adapter separates its task data, as measured by the unnormalized margin. In practice, however, datasets are often not perfectly separable, so the minimum margin C ⁡ ( ⋅ , ⋅ ) C(\cdot;\cdot) can be negative and overly sensitive to hard examples. We therefore use the average margin C ¯ ​ ( ⋅ , 𝒟 ) \bar{C}(\cdot;\mathcal{D}) as a more stable proxy for adapter performance. Under the strict-orthogonal assumptions of Theorem 3.3 , the per-sample margins of each optimal adapter are equal on its own fine-tuning dataset. Consequently, minimum and average margins coincide on these fine-tuning datasets. In our practical algorithm, we therefore use average margins as empirical proxies for the minimum margins appearing in the theoretical mixing rule.

Motivated by Theorem 3.3 , we propose a practical LoRA merging algorithm using the average-margin proxies C ¯ ​ ( W , 𝒟 ) \bar{C}(W;\mathcal{D}) . When a task has non-positive average margin C ¯ i \bar{C}_{i} , the corresponding coefficient would be negative and no longer consistent with the regime motivated by the theorem. Algorithm 1 therefore drops such tasks by setting their coefficients to zero. We also tune a global scaling factor s ∗ s^{\ast} on a held-out validation set, following Ilharco et al. (2022) , and find that this further improves performance. In § 4.2 , we compare the resulting method with other popular adapter-merging baselines.

Our experiments aim to validate the theoretical predictions in Section 3 and assess how well they transfer beyond the linear setting, rather than to establish state-of-the-art performance. Since our analysis gives closed-form predictions for optimal regularization and adapter mixing coefficients, we test whether these quantities match empirical behavior in modern architectures. Specifically, we focus on two questions: (i) whether the mixing coefficients derived from our margin analysis agree with empirically optimal coefficients, and (ii) whether the resulting theory-driven merging rule, MaLoRA, remains competitive with adapter-merging baselines in nonlinear models. Experiments on the effect of regularization are deferred to Appendix H.1.2 .

Setup and metric. We evaluate our theory and method in two complementary settings. First, in linear probing on CIFAR-100 ( Krizhevsky et al., 2009 ) (§ 4.1 ), we use four frozen pre-trained backbones ( ResNet-50 , ViT-B/16 , ConvNeXt , and CLIP ) as feature extractors ( He et al., 2016 ; Dosovitskiy et al., 2021 ; Radford et al., 2021 ; Liu et al., 2022 ) , apply LoRA only to the final linear classifier ( Kornblith et al., 2019 ) , and construct tasks from the CIFAR-100 superclass hierarchy. Second, in multi-domain adapter merging (§ 4.2 ), we evaluate ViT-B/16 on PACS, VLCS, and TerraIncognita ( Fang et al., 2013 ; Li et al., 2017 ; Beery et al., 2018 ) , and XLM-RoBERTa Base on MNLI, Amazon Reviews, and CivilComments ( Zhang et al., 2015 ; Williams et al., 2018 ; Borkan et al., 2019 ; Conneau et al., 2020 ) . Although our theory is stated in terms of normalized margin, we report classification accuracy in experiments, since real-world classification tasks often do not achieve perfect separation and can have negative normalized margins. Additional details are given in Appendix H .

In this work, we study LoRA fine-tuning through the normalized margin under a near-orthogonal task regime. We characterize the global minimizer of the regularized LoRA objective across three regularization regimes (Theorem 3.1 ), derive closed-form expressions for the margins on the pre-training and fine-tuning data, and identify the regularization level that maximizes the margin on their union (Theorem 3.2 ). We further extend the analysis to multi-task settings by deriving closed-form optimal mixing coefficients for adapter merging (Theorem 3.3 ). Based on this theory, we propose margin-based LoRA merging (MaLoRA, Algorithm 1 ), which matches or outperforms several adapter-merging baselines on a range of vision and language benchmarks. Across architectures and tasks, the empirical results closely align with the theoretical predictions. Limitations and future work. First, our analysis relies on simplifying assumptions, most notably near-orthogonal task structure (Assumption 2.1 ) and balanced class sizes in the fine-tuning data. These assumptions enable a sharp closed-form characterization, but they also limit the scope of the theory. An important direction for future work is to relax them and study LoRA under more general data distributions and pre-training conditions. Second, experiments applying MaLoRA to nonlinear models provide empirical support for the practical usefulness of our merging rule beyond multiclass linear classification. These findings motivate extending the margin-based theoretical analysis to nonlinear adaptation. Third, our theory characterizes margins on the training datasets; establishing corresponding generalization or test-risk guarantees requires further analysis.

Theory of LoRA. There are many works theoretically studying the expressiveness, characterizing the loss landscape, and understanding the learning dynamics of LoRA. Zeng and Lee [2023] prove that, under mild assumptions, LoRA can approximate any deep linear, feed-forward, or transformer network. Within the NTK regime, Malladi et al. [2023] characterize the conditions under which one can study LoRA in the NTK regime, while Jang et al. [2024] show that when the LoRA rank is r i ≳ N r_{i}\gtrsim\sqrt{N} , where N N is the number of samples, the optimization landscape of LoRA has no spurious local minima, and GD can find 𝒪 ⁡ ( N ) \mathcal{O}(\sqrt{N}) -rank solutions that generalize well. Moreover, Xu et al. [2025] study the learning dynamics of LoRA in the context of matrix factorization, and show that smaller initialization leads to longer training time and lower training error. However, none of these studies theoretically characterize why LoRA reduces catastrophic forgetting and support effective adapter merging .

LoRA merging. A variety of techniques have been proposed to merge task-specific LoRA adapters by forming a weighted average of their parameters. For example, LoRA-Hub [ Huang et al., 2023 ] learns per-task mixing coefficients first, and then applies a weighted average of LoRA weight matrices B B and A A separately. LoRA-Flow [ Wang et al., 2024 ] introduces token-level gates that dynamically assign merging coefficients to each LoRA adapter before taking weighted averaging. LoRA-Retriever [ Zhao et al., 2024 ] first retrieves the most relevant adapters for each input, and then averages the selected LoRA adapters. Beyond weighted averaging, another line of work attempts to address redundancy and conflicting updates directly. TIES [ Yadav et al., 2023 ] proceeds in three steps: trimming redundant parameters, resolving sign conflicts into an aggregate vector, and averaging only the parameters consistent with the aggregate sign, thereby mitigating degradation from redundant or conflicting updates. DARE [ Yu et al., 2024 ] can be used as a preprocessing step for other merging methods, where parameters are randomly dropped according to a specified rate and the remaining ones are rescaled, reducing redundancy and potential interference among merged adapters. However, all these methods remain largely heuristic and lack theoretical guarantees.

Regularization and task orthogonality help reduce forgetting. A large body of work in fine-tuning and continual learning shows that controlling deviation of the fine-tuned model from the pretrained model reduces catastrophic forgetting. Concretely, these approaches impose weight-space penalties that restrict the magnitude and direction of parameter updates away from the pretrained solution. Weight-anchoring and importance-aware penalties exemplify this idea: Kirkpatrick et al. [2017] penalize movement along directions identified by the Fisher information matrix, while Zenke et al. [2017] accumulate path-wise importance during training. Schwarz et al. [2018] extend this idea to long sequences of tasks. Related approaches estimate parameter sensitivity [ Aljundi et al., 2018 ] , apply output-level distillation to preserve prior behavior [ Li and Hoiem, 2016 ] , or explicitly regularize parameters toward the pretrained anchor [ Li et al., 2018 ] . Although these approaches differ in how importance or anchoring is computed, the common mechanism is the same: weight-space regularizers constrain updates during fine-tuning relative to the pretrained model to mitigate catastrophic forgetting . Another complementary perspective highlights the role of task relations. When task representations are sufficiently decorrelated, interference between tasks is naturally reduced and forgetting is alleviated. In linear and kernelized models, it has been shown that when tasks are orthogonal or nearly orthogonal, cross-task gradient interference vanishes in expectation, implying negligible forgetting [ Doan et al., 2021 , Evron et al., 2022 ] . These insights resonate with our analysis of LoRA, where we explicitly study a regularized objective on low-rank adapters and make the simplifying

This assumption directly connects to prior findings on task orthogonality and provides a tractable setting in which we can isolate and analyze the role of regularization in mitigating forgetting.

chunks.section: Appendix E Proof of Theorem 3.2 and Corollary 3.1
chunks.text: In this section, we first present the proofs of Theorem 3.2 and Corollary 3.1 . Then, under additional smallness assumptions on ϵ 1 , ϵ 2 \epsilon_{1},\epsilon_{2} , we show that the same conclusions still hold, with additional error terms that depend on ϵ 1 , ϵ 2 \epsilon_{1},\epsilon_{2} .

For convenience, we will first define the following notations. Let W LoRA λ = W pre + B λ ∗ ​ A λ ∗ W_{\mathrm{LoRA}}^{\lambda}=W_{\mathrm{pre}}+B_{\lambda}^{\ast}A_{\lambda}^{\ast} , and define the following shorthand for margins as: γ pre = γ ⁡ ( W pre , 𝒟 pre ) \gamma_{\mathrm{pre}}=\gamma(W_{\mathrm{pre}};\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pre}}) , γ ft , λ = γ ⁡ ( B λ ∗ ​ A λ ∗ , 𝒟 ft ) \gamma_{\mathrm{ft},\lambda}=\gamma(B_{\lambda}^{\ast}A_{\lambda}^{\ast};\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{ft}}) , and γ λ = γ ⁡ ( W LoRA λ , 𝒟 pre ∪ 𝒟 ft ) \gamma_{\lambda}=\gamma(W_{\mathrm{LoRA}}^{\lambda};\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pre}}\cup\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{ft}}) . Additionally, given an K ¯ \bar{K} -class max-margin classifier W ft ∗ ∈ ℝ K ¯ × d W_{\mathrm{ft}}^{\ast}\in\mathbb{R}^{\bar{K}\times d} on the fine-tuning data, let γ ft pad = γ ⁡ ( ( [ W ft ∗ ; 0 ( K − K ¯ ) × d ] ) , 𝒟 ft ) \gamma_{\mathrm{ft}}^{\mathrm{pad}}=\gamma(([W_{\mathrm{ft}}^{\ast};\,\bm{0}_{(K-\bar{K})\times d}]);\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{ft}}) . When K ¯ < K \bar{K}<K this is in general a lower bound on max W ∈ ℝ K × d ⁡ γ ⁡ ( W , 𝒟 ft ) \max_{W\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times d}}\gamma(W;\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{ft}}) , with equality iff K ¯ = K \bar{K}=K . In the balanced case K ¯ = K \bar{K}=K , γ ft pad = γ ft ∗ \gamma_{\mathrm{ft}}^{\mathrm{pad}}=\gamma_{\mathrm{ft}}^{\ast} as defined in the main theorem.

With these definitions in place, we restate Theorem 3.2 in expanded form covering the general K ¯ ≤ K \bar{K}\!\leq\!K setting. The expanded version specifies the closed-form values of Θ λ \Theta_{\lambda} and γ ft , λ \gamma_{\mathrm{ft},\lambda} in three regimes when K ¯ < K \bar{K}\!<\!K . In the balanced case K ¯ = K \bar{K}\!=\!K , the intermediate and low-penalty regimes coincide in their ETF geometry and margin formulas, recovering the two-regime statement of Theorem 3.2 . More precisely, λ crit = 0 \lambda_{\mathrm{crit}}\!=\!0 , so the intermediate formula holds for every < λ < 1 / ( K ​ n ) 0\!<\!\lambda\!<\!1/(K\sqrt{n}) , and the limit λ → 0 + \lambda\!\to\!0^{+} retains the same ETF geometry.

Adopt the setup of Theorem 3.1 and let Θ λ := ‖ B λ ∗ ​ A λ ∗ ‖ F \Theta_{\lambda}\!:=\!\|B^{\ast}_{\lambda}A^{\ast}_{\lambda}\|_{F} . The normalized margins of W LoRA λ W_{\mathrm{LoRA}}^{\lambda} on the pre-training and fine-tuning data are γ ⁡ ( W LoRA λ , 𝒟 pre ) = γ pre ​ ρ pre Θ λ 2 + ρ pre 2 , γ ⁡ ( W LoRA λ , 𝒟 ft ) = γ ft , λ ​ Θ λ Θ λ 2 + ρ pre 2 , \displaystyle\gamma\bigl(W_{\mathrm{LoRA}}^{\lambda};\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pre}}\bigr)=\gamma_{\mathrm{pre}}\,\frac{\rho_{\mathrm{pre}}}{\sqrt{\Theta_{\lambda}^{2}+\rho_{\mathrm{pre}}^{2}}}\,,\quad\gamma\bigl(W_{\mathrm{LoRA}}^{\lambda};\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{ft}}\bigr)=\gamma_{\mathrm{ft,\lambda}}\,\frac{\Theta_{\lambda}}{\sqrt{\Theta_{\lambda}^{2}+\rho_{\mathrm{pre}}^{2}}}\,, (62) which yield the closed-form Adapt ⁡ ( λ ) \mathrm{Adapt}(\lambda) and Forget ⁡ ( λ ) \mathrm{Forget}(\lambda) in ( 13 ) via Adapt ⁡ ( λ ) = γ ⁡ ( W LoRA λ , 𝒟 ft ) \mathrm{Adapt}(\lambda)=\gamma(W_{\mathrm{LoRA}}^{\lambda};\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{ft}}) (since γ ⁡ ( W pre , 𝒟 ft ) = 0 \gamma(W_{\mathrm{pre}};\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{ft}})=0 in the strict-orthogonal regime) and Forget ⁡ ( λ ) = γ pre − γ ⁡ ( W LoRA λ , 𝒟 pre ) \mathrm{Forget}(\lambda)=\gamma_{\mathrm{pre}}-\gamma(W_{\mathrm{LoRA}}^{\lambda};\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pre}}) . Moreover, Θ λ \Theta_{\lambda} and γ ft , λ \gamma_{\mathrm{ft},\lambda} take the following values: (i) High–penalty regime λ ≥ 1 K ¯ ​ n \lambda\geq\frac{1}{\bar{K}\sqrt{n}} : Θ λ = γ ft , λ = 0 \Theta_{\lambda}=\gamma_{\mathrm{ft},\lambda}=0 , and hence Adapt ⁡ ( λ ) = Forget ⁡ ( λ ) = 0 \mathrm{Adapt}(\lambda)=\mathrm{Forget}(\lambda)=0 .

(ii) Intermediate regime λ crit < λ < 1 K ¯ ​ n \lambda_{\mathrm{crit}}<\lambda<\frac{1}{\bar{K}\sqrt{n}} : Θ λ = ρ λ K ¯ − 1 \Theta_{\lambda}=\frac{\rho_{\lambda}}{\sqrt{\bar{K}-1}} , γ ft , λ = γ ft pad \gamma_{\mathrm{ft,\lambda}}=\gamma_{\mathrm{ft}}^{\mathrm{pad}} , and Θ λ \Theta_{\lambda} is a strictly decreasing function of λ \lambda . Both Adapt ⁡ ( λ ) \mathrm{Adapt}(\lambda) and Forget ⁡ ( λ ) \mathrm{Forget}(\lambda) are therefore strictly decreasing in λ \lambda on this regime. (iii) Low–penalty regime < λ ≤ λ crit 0\!<\!\lambda\!\leq\!\lambda_{\mathrm{crit}} : Θ λ = n ​ K ¯ ​ a λ 2 + n ​ K ¯ ​ ( K ¯ − 1 ) ​ b λ 2 + n ​ K ¯ ​ ( K − K ¯ ) ​ c λ 2 , γ ft , λ = a λ + c λ Θ λ . \displaystyle\Theta_{\lambda}=\sqrt{n\bar{K}a_{\lambda}^{2}+n\bar{K}(\bar{K}-1)b_{\lambda}^{2}+n\bar{K}(K-\bar{K})c_{\lambda}^{2}}\,,\quad\gamma_{\mathrm{ft},\lambda}=\frac{a_{\lambda}+c_{\lambda}}{\Theta_{\lambda}}\,.

Full fine-tuning as an alternative method. While our work focuses on LoRA, it is instructive to briefly contrast it with the more conventional strategy of full fine-tuning. Full fine-tuning updates all parameters of the pretrained model, which is considerably less efficient in both computation and storage, whereas LoRA achieves adaptation through a compact low-rank parameterization. In the linear classification setting, the two approaches correspond to the following regularized objectives: min B , A ⁡ L ⁡ ( W pre + B ​ A , 𝒟 ft ) + λ 2 ​ ( ‖ B ‖ F 2 + ‖ A ‖ F 2 ) , \displaystyle\min_{B,A}\;L\!\left(W_{\mathrm{pre}}+BA;\,\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{ft}}\right)+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\!\left(\|B\|_{F}^{2}+\|A\|_{F}^{2}\right)\,, LoRA objective , \displaystyle\text{LoRA objective}\,, (63) min W ⁡ L ⁡ ( W , 𝒟 ft ) + λ 2 ​ ‖ W − W pre ‖ F 2 , \displaystyle\min_{W}\;L\!\left(W;\,\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{ft}}\right)+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\|W-W_{\mathrm{pre}}\|_{F}^{2}\,, Full fine-tuning objective . \displaystyle\text{Full fine-tuning objective}\,. (64) Beyond efficiency, the two formulations induce fundamentally different (implicit) biases. By exploiting the variational form of the nuclear norm [ Recht et al., 2010 ] , one can show that for any solution ( B ∗ , A ∗ ) (B^{\ast},A^{\ast}) of ( 63 ), the induced update W LoRA λ W_{\mathrm{LoRA}}^{\lambda} is equivalently the solution of min W , rank ⁡ ( W − W pre ) ≤ r ⁡ L ⁡ ( W , 𝒟 ft ) + λ ​ ‖ W − W pre ‖ ∗ , Implicit bias of LoRA fine-tuning , \displaystyle\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}W,\mathrm{rank}(W-W_{\mathrm{pre}})\leq r\end{subarray}}\;L\!\left(W;\,\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{ft}}\right)+\lambda\|W-W_{\mathrm{pre}}\|_{\ast}\,,\qquad\text{Implicit bias of LoRA fine-tuning}\,, (65)

which highlights LoRA’s connection to nuclear-norm regularization under rank constraints. We refer the readers to Jang et al. [2024] for the proof of the argument. Understanding the consequences of this distinction between nuclear norm regularization and Frobenius norm regularization remains an open direction for future work. Importantly, our goal is not to compare LoRA and full fine-tuning, but to rigorously analyze why LoRA exhibits reduced forgetting and to provide principled guidance for selecting regularization parameters in adapter-based fine-tuning.

In this section, we present the detailed setup of the experiments in § 4 . Code availability. Code is available at https://github.com/simonxu97/MaLoRA . Hardware. All experiments are run on a single NVIDIA RTXA5000 GPU (24GB) per (benchmark, seed), allocated through an academic SLURM cluster. The backbones—ViT-Base/16 pre-trained on ImageNet-21k and XLM-RoBERTa Base—are loaded directly from public checkpoints; we do not pretrain any model from scratch. Per-domain LoRA finetuning runs for 20 20 fixed epochs with AdamW and takes 5–30 minutes per domain depending on the dataset, totalling roughly 0.5–3GPU-hours per (benchmark, seed) across all per-domain adapters and the pretrain-task adapter. Computational overhead and merge-selection runtime are reported in Appendix H.2.2 , using a dedicated matched-budget timing protocol.

Specifically, for each class we randomly sample 100 points (10,000 in total). We first report the distribution of pairwise cosine similarities across all sampled points in Figure 2 . For intra-class similarities, we randomly sample up to 1,000 distinct sample pairs per class (drawn without replacement to exclude trivial self-pairs whose cosine would be 1 1 ); for inter-class similarities, we sample up to 1,000 pairs for each class pair. In this section, we numerically verify Theorem 3.2 . We first pre-train a linear classifier on the pretraining task, and then fine-tune it using LoRA across 50 logarithmically spaced regularization strengths, with λ ∈ [ 10 − 5 , 10 − 1 ] \lambda\in[10^{-5},10^{-1}] . Figure 4 shows that LoRA’s performance exhibits a non-monotonic relationship with λ \lambda , peaking at a moderate value. 1. Claims Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The claim made in the abstract can be found in Theorem 3.1 , Theorem 3.2 , Theorem 3.3 , and Algorithm 1 . Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper. • The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers. • The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings. • It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper. 2. Limitations Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors? Answer: [Yes] Justification: we discuss the limitations of the work in § 5 . Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper. • The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper. • The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.

• The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated. • The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon. • The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size. • If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness. • While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations. 3. Theory assumptions and proofs Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof? Answer: [Yes] Justification: we list all the assumptions in § 2.1 , and provide proofs in Appendix D –Appendix F . Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results.

• All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced. • All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems. • The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition. • Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material. • Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced. 4. Experimental result reproducibility Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: we list all the model architectures, datasets, and training setups in Appendix H . Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not. • If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable.

• Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed. • While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example (a) If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm. (b) If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully. (c) If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset).

(d) We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results. 5. Open access to data and code Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material? Answer: [Yes] Justification: all the experiments conducted in this paper use open source datasets, and we provide citations to them. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code. • Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines ( https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy ) for more details. • While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source benchmark). • The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines ( https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy ) for more details. • The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc.

• The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why. • At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable). • Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted. 6. Experimental setting/details Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results? Answer: [Yes] Justification: in Appendix H , we provide details on the experiments. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them. • The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material. 7. Experiment statistical significance Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: in Appendix H , we report the mean normalized accuracy and drop with std computed based on 10 repetitions. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper.

• The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions). • The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.) • The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors). • It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean. • It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified. • For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates). • If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text. 8. Experiments compute resources Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: we report the usage of computational resources in Appendix H . Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage.

• The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute. • The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didn’t make it into the paper). 9. Code of ethics Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines ? Answer: [Yes] Justification: we have reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics and followed it. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics. • If the authors answer [No] , they should explain the special circumstances that require a deviation from the Code of Ethics. • The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is a special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction). 10. Broader impacts Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed? Answer: [N/A] Justification: there is no societal impact of the work performed. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed. • If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact. • Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations.

• The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. links.context: Foundation models have transformed artificial intelligence across numerous domains. However, deploying these models in real-world applications typically requires fine-tuning on specialized datasets to meet accuracy, safety, and alignment requirements. Traditional full fine-tuning, which updates all parameters of a pre-trained model, incurs substantial computational cost, including large memory footprints, long training times, and significant storage demands. Paper contributions. We study LoRA in multiclass linear classification under a near-orthogonal-task regime, in which fine-tuning samples are nearly orthogonal to one another and to the pre-training samples. In this setting, we characterize the global minimizer of the LoRA objective and use this characterization to analyze forgetting and adapter merging.
